title: Judges 2:6–10
context: The narrator now looks back. When Joshua had sent the people away, the children of Israel each went to his inheritance to possess the land. The people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived him and had seen all the great work of the LORD that he had worked for Israel. Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died at the age of one hundred ten. They buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath Heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash. After that generation was gathered to their fathers, another generation arose who did not know the LORD, nor the work which he had done for Israel. The unit closely parallels the close of Joshua, including Joshua’s death, burial, and the faithfulness of his generation. Judges names the burial place Timnath Heres, while Joshua uses a slightly different form of the name; the two are commonly taken as the same place, and that identification should be treated as a common reading, not as a point to be pressed into a contradiction or a forced proof. How this recap sits after the opening “After the death of Joshua,” and after Bochim is a literary question (a flashback or resume before the cycle is described). Both traditions read the contrast between the generation that saw the LORD’s work and the generation that did not know him as the hinge into verses 11–23.

verses.text: Now when Joshua had sent the people away, the children of Israel each went to his inheritance to possess the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
Now when Joshua had sent the people away, the children of Israel each went to his inheritance to possess the land. The narrator steps back to the dismissal under Joshua and to the going out into the lots.

Arminian readers hear a real sending and a real taking up of the inheritance. Each goes to possess; the later failures of chapter 1 are not written back onto this earlier going as if no faithful start had ever been made.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers take the “Now when” as a look back to Joshua’s sending, a resume that will explain how the people once stood and how they will fall. Possession of the inheritance begins under that dismissal.

Both traditions read the verse as a recap of the settlement, shared ground with the end of Joshua, without a contrast over the literary seam itself.

verses.text: The people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work of the LORD that he had worked for Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
The people served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great work of the LORD that he had worked for Israel. Service is joined to living memory of what God had done.

Arminian readers hear a generation that actually served, and they hear why: they had seen the LORD’s great work. The next generation will be responsible to know that work too; seeing is not automatically inherited.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress that the service lasted as long as Joshua and the witnessing elders lived. The LORD’s great work, once seen, held a generation in the way; the verse already prepares for the loss that verse 10 will name.

Both traditions take this faithfulness as real, and as bound to remembered works, shared ground rather than a dispute about that generation’s sincerity.

verses.text: Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being one hundred ten years old.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being one hundred ten years old. The honorific given to Moses is here given to Joshua, and his age is recorded.

Arminian readers hear the end of a faithful servant’s life. The title does not make him more than a servant; it marks a finished stewardship, after which Israel must still serve the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise linger over “the servant of the LORD,” and Joshua’s death at one hundred ten closes the era verse 7 has just praised; the book’s crisis will not be the lack of a second Joshua so much as the lack of knowledge of the LORD.

Both traditions read the death notice as the honorable end of that servant’s work, shared ground at a grave that verse 9 will locate.

verses.text: They buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath Heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, on the north of the mountain of Gaash.
verses.arminianNotes:
They buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnath Heres, in the hill country of Ephraim, on the north of the mountain of Gaash. The servant is laid in his own lot, in a named place.

Arminian readers hear a particular burial, not a legend without a site. Joshua rests in the inheritance he received. The book of Joshua uses a slightly different form of the town’s name; the two are commonly taken as the same place, a common identification rather than a proven puzzle or a contradiction.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take Timnath Heres, in Ephraim, north of Gaash, as the burial the narrator wishes to record. The slightly different name in Joshua is often read as the same town; that should remain a common way of holding the notices together, not a consensus declared beyond the evidence.

Both traditions receive the grave as the close of Joshua’s inheritance, without a contrast over the name.

verses.text: After all that generation were gathered to their fathers, another generation arose after them who didn’t know the LORD, nor the work which he had done for Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
After all that generation were gathered to their fathers, another generation arose after them who “didn’t know the LORD, nor the work which he had done for Israel.” The hinge of the opening is this not-knowing.

Arminian readers hear a new generation that is really responsible. Knowledge of the LORD and of his work is not inherited by blood; each generation must know him, and this one does not. The failure is more than a lack of private information; they do not acknowledge the LORD or what he had done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same break. The generation that had seen the work is gathered to its fathers, and the next does not know the LORD or that work. Verse 7’s memory was meant to be the means of holding the people; when it is gone, the cycle of verses 11–23 can begin.

Both traditions take the not-knowing as the moral and spiritual turn of the book, shared ground, not a contrast over whether the ignorance was only intellectual or also a refusal to acknowledge God. It is at least the latter, and both can say so.
